Streaming data: A continuous, unbounded sequence of events generated in real time by sources like IoT devices, sensors, or transactions. Unlike batch data, it has no fixed end and must be processed on the fly as it arrives.
Batch processing: Collecting data into a finite chunk (a file, a table, a query result) and processing it all at once, typically on a schedule. The job ends when the data is exhausted — the opposite of an open-ended stream.
Unbounded: Having no defined end. A streaming source is unbounded: the consumer keeps running and waits for the next event rather than finishing when the current data runs out.
Publish/subscribe: A messaging pattern where producers (publishers) send messages to a named destination and any number of consumers (subscribers) register interest and receive them. Producers and consumers are decoupled — neither needs to know about the other.
Broker: The server that receives messages from producers and delivers them to subscribed consumers. HiveMQ, EMQX, and RabbitMQ are brokers; Kafka brokers play the same role in a cluster.
Topic: A named channel on a broker that messages are published to and consumed from. Subscribers express interest in a topic to receive its messages.
Producer: A client that publishes messages to a broker (for example a sensor script, or Pentaho Data Integration's MQTT producer step).
Consumer: A client that subscribes to a stream and reads messages from it. In Pentaho Data Integration the consumer steps are MQTT consumer, Kafka consumer, and AMQP consumer.
Parent/child transformation: The Pentaho Data Integration streaming pattern. The parent transformation holds the consumer step, which collects incoming messages into batches; each batch is handed to a child transformation that processes the records. The same pattern is used for every streaming protocol.
Get records from stream: The Pentaho Data Integration step that surfaces a batch of streamed messages as rows. It produces rows, so it must be the first step in the child transformation; you cannot place it mid-stream.
Batch (streaming): A group of messages the consumer collects before invoking the child transformation. It is flushed when the first threshold is met — either a Duration (ms) time window or a Number of records count.
MQTT: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport — a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol designed for the Internet of Things. Minimal overhead suits constrained devices and sensor networks.
QoS: Quality of Service in MQTT, controlling delivery guarantees: 0 (at most once, lowest latency, can lose messages), 1 (at least once, may duplicate), 2 (exactly once, highest overhead).
Clean session: An MQTT connection flag. When true the broker keeps no state for the client; when false the broker persists the client's subscriptions and queued QoS 1/2 messages between connections.
HiveMQ: An enterprise MQTT broker used in this course to carry industrial robot-sensor telemetry. Runs as a Podman container exposing its TCP listener on port 1883 and a Control Center on 9090.
EMQX: A scalable open-source MQTT broker used in the logistics / predictive-maintenance workshop. Exposes an MQTT TCP listener on 1884, beside HiveMQ on 1883, and a dashboard on 18083.
SCADA: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition — software and hardware systems that gather and control data from industrial equipment. Most SCADA and MES systems support MQTT, making it the natural ingestion protocol for factory telemetry.
IoT: Internet of Things — networks of connected devices and sensors that publish data, often over lightweight protocols like MQTT because of their limited memory and power.
Apache Kafka: A distributed event-streaming platform for high-volume, fault-tolerant publish/subscribe pipelines. Built around a distributed commit log, it provides durability and high throughput for producers and consumers.
KRaft: Kafka Raft metadata mode — Kafka's controller architecture that removes the ZooKeeper dependency by managing cluster metadata within Kafka itself using the Raft consensus protocol, simplifying deployment.
Partition: A Kafka topic is split into partitions — ordered, append-only logs. Partitions allow a topic to scale across brokers and let consumers in a group divide the work.
Offset: A sequential ID that uniquely identifies a record within a Kafka partition. Consumers track offsets to know what they have read and where to resume.
Consumer group: A set of Kafka consumers that cooperate to read a topic. Each consumer in the group is assigned a subset of the topic's partitions, so the group shares the load.
auto.offset.reset: A Kafka consumer option that sets where to begin reading when no committed offset exists: earliest (from the start of the topic) or latest (only new messages).
Schema Registry: A centralized repository, separate from the brokers, that stores and validates the schemas describing topic messages, and handles serialization/deserialization. It uses Kafka as its durable backend.
AMQP: Advanced Message Queuing Protocol — a standardized, open broker protocol for reliable, decoupled messaging. Supports asynchronous communication, system decoupling, resilience, and load balancing.
RabbitMQ: An open-source message broker that implements AMQP. Used in this course to carry room-sensor data (temperature, pressure, humidity) through the default exchange to the durable queue tv_room.
Exchange: In AMQP, the entity a producer publishes to. The exchange routes messages to queues using bindings and routing keys, rather than the producer writing to a queue directly.
Binding: A link between an exchange and a queue that tells the exchange which messages to route to that queue.
Routing key: A message attribute the exchange inspects to decide how to route a message to queues. With DIRECT or TOPIC exchange types you specify one or more routing keys.
Fanout: A RabbitMQ exchange type that broadcasts every message it receives to all bound queues, ignoring routing keys. (The default exchange is a direct exchange.)
Queue: In AMQP, the structure that stores messages until a consumer retrieves them. Queues can be durable (survive restarts), exclusive (one connection), or auto-delete (removed when the last consumer disconnects).
Durable: A broker object (queue or exchange) configured to be saved to disk so it survives a broker restart, as opposed to a transient object that is lost. A durable queue's messages survive a restart only if they were published as persistent.
MQTT Producer: The Pentaho Data Integration step that publishes a message field to an MQTT broker on a given topic, with configurable QoS and client ID.
Backpressure: Controls that prevent a fast stream from overwhelming the consumer — for example the message prefetch limit (how many messages Pentaho Data Integration queues in memory) and the maximum concurrent batches.
Acknowledgment (ack): A consumer's confirmation to the broker that it has taken a message, after which the broker can delete it. On the Batch tab of the AMQP consumer step, Ack when message received confirms each message as it arrives; Ack when batch completed confirms a batch's messages only after the child transformation has finished with them.
At-least-once delivery: A delivery guarantee under which no record is lost but one can arrive twice: if a consumer stops between processing a record and committing its offset, the record is delivered again. In the Kafka lab, the table's unique key on topic, partition and offset, with Ignore insert errors on Table output, keeps one row per record.
Shared subscription: An MQTT subscription to `$share/<group>/<topic>`: the subscribers in the group share the topic, and the broker hands each message to one of them. MQTT's way to scale out consumers, like a Kafka consumer group.
Authenticator: In EMQX, a check in the authentication chain, such as a password lookup in its built-in database. With none configured every client may connect; with one, a client it does not accept is refused.
Unified Namespace: One MQTT topic tree for the whole business, usually shaped like the ISA-95 hierarchy (enterprise, site, line, device, message), where every device publishes its current data and every application finds it by place.
Sparkplug B: An Eclipse Foundation specification on top of MQTT: fixed `spBv1.0/...` topics, birth and death messages for device state, and binary Protobuf payloads.
Data contract: The agreed shape of a stream's messages: which fields, of which types, with which values. The consumer checks it; a message that breaks it is rejected, not loaded.
Poison message: A message that stops a consumer every time it is read. Its batch is never committed, so the pipeline cannot pass it until the message is routed aside.
Dead-letter topic: A topic that receives the messages a pipeline refuses, unchanged and with the reason, so they can be read, fixed and sent again. In the course: `pdi-signups-rejects`.
Consumer lag: How far a consumer group is behind: the end of the log minus the group's committed offset, per partition.
Replay: Reading a topic's records again by moving a consumer group's committed offset back, for example to rebuild a table after fixing a pipeline. Safe only where every write can happen twice.
Stream processor: An engine, such as Apache Flink or Kafka Streams, that handles each event as it arrives and keeps state between events, for windows and joins over time.
Change data capture: Reading inserts, updates and deletes from a database's transaction log and publishing each change as an event, without changing the application that made it.
